{{Short description|Japanese syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism}} {{Italic title|reason=}} {{Shinto}}{{Refimprove|date=October 2023}}[[File:Inari-Jogyo-ji.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Kitsune|en|Kitsune|WD=Q692111|lt=Foxes|1=Kitsune}} sacred to Shinto kami {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|WD=Q719665|lt=Inari|1=Inari Ōkami}}, a ''[[torii]]'', a Buddhist [[Japanese pagoda|stone pagoda]], and Buddhist figures together at Jōgyō-ji, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura}}.]] '''''Shinbutsu-shūgō''''' ({{lang|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}, "syncretism of [[kami]] and buddhas"), also called '''Shinbutsu shū''' ({{lang|ja|神仏宗}}, "kami and {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=The Buddha|1=The Buddha}} school") '''Shinbutsu-konkō''' ({{lang|ja|神仏混淆}}, "jumbling up" or "contamination of kami and buddhas"), is the {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=Syncretism|1=Syncretism}} of [[Shinto]] and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}} that was Japan's main organized religion up until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period|1=Meiji era}}. Beginning in 1868, the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government|1=Government of Meiji Japan}} approved a series of laws that separated Japanese native [[kami]] worship, on one side, from Buddhism which had assimilated it, on the other.
When Buddhism was introduced from {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China|1=China}} in the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|WD=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}} (6th century), the Japanese tried to reconcile the new beliefs with the older [[Shinto]] beliefs, assuming both were true. As a consequence, {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples|1=Buddhist temples in Japan}} ({{lang|ja|寺}}, ''tera'') were {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=attached|1=Jingū-ji}} to local {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}}s ({{lang|ja|神社}}, ''jinja'') and vice versa and devoted to both [[kami]] and {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=Buddhist figures|1=Buddhahood}}. The local religion and foreign Buddhism never fused into a single, unified religion, but remained inextricably linked to the present day through interaction. The depth of the influence from Buddhism on local religious beliefs can be seen in much of Shinto's conceptual vocabulary and even the types of Shinto shrines seen today. The large worship halls and religious images are themselves of Buddhist origin.<ref name="Tamura21">Tamura, page 21</ref> The formal [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Buddhism from Shinto]] took place only as recently as the end of the 19th century; however, in many ways, the blending of the two still continues.<ref name="sueki2"/>
The term ''shinbutsu shūgō'' itself was coined during the early modern era (17th century) to refer to the amalgamation of kami and buddhas in general, as opposed to specific currents within Buddhism which did the same, e.g. Ryōbu Shintō and Sannō Shintō.<ref name=inoue>Inoue (2004:67-68)</ref> The term may have a negative connotation of bastardization and randomness.<ref>Teeuwen & Rambelli (2002:49)</ref> It is a {{ill|Yojijukugo|en|Yojijukugo|WD=Q7010524|lt=Yojijukugo|1=Yojijukugo}} phrase.
==Assimilation of Buddhism==
===Debate over the nature of Shinto=== There is no agreement among specialists as to the exact extent of fusion between the two religions.<ref name="BT4"/>
According to some scholars (such as Hirai Naofusa in Japan and {{ill|Joseph Kitagawa|en|Joseph Kitagawa|WD=Q3185165|lt=Joseph Kitagawa|1=Joseph Kitagawa}} in the US), Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, has existed as such continuously since its prehistory, and consists of all the uniquely Japanese rituals and beliefs shaped by Japanese history from prehistory to the present.<ref name="BT4"/> The term "Shinto" itself was coined in the 6th century to differentiate the previously disparate local religious practices from imported Buddhism.<ref name="KG139">Kitagawa (1987:139)</ref>
The opposing view of Japanese historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en|Toshio Kuroda|WD=Q130309955|lt=Toshio Kuroda|1=Toshio Kuroda}}<ref>{{citation |last=Kuroda |first=Toshio |contribution=Shinto in the History of Japanese Religion |date=1981 |contribution-url=http://www.univie.ac.at/rel_jap/k/images/0/03/Kuroda_1981.pdf |translator-last=Dobbins |translator-first=James C. |translator2-last=Gay |translator2-first=Suzanne |display-translators=1 |title=Journal of Japanese Studies |volume=7 |issue=1 }}.</ref> and his supporters is that Shinto as an independent religion was born only in the modern period after emerging in the Middle Ages as an offshoot of Buddhism,<ref name="BT4">Breen and Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:4-5)</ref><ref name="rambelli">Rambelli (2001)</ref> and that Shinto as a distinct religion is a Meiji era invention of Japanese nationalist ideologues.<ref name="BT4"/> Kuroda points out how the state formalization of ''[[kami]]'' rituals and the state Ranking of shrines during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} were not the emergence of Shinto as an independent religion, but an effort to explain local beliefs in Buddhist terms.<ref name="BT4"/> He also says that, while it is true that the two characters for "Shinto" appear very early in the historical record (for example in the [[Nihon Shoki]]), this does not mean today's Shinto already existed as a religion because the same word was originally used for [[Taoism]] or even for religion in general.<ref name="BT4"/> Indeed, according to Kuroda, many features of Shinto (for example the worshiping of mirrors and swords or the very structure of the [[Ise Grand Shrine]], Shinto's holiest and most important site) are typical of Taoism.<ref name="BT4"/> The term "Shinto" in old texts, therefore, does not necessarily indicate something uniquely Japanese.
Still, according to this view, Shinto's rise as an autonomous religion was gradual and started to become evident with the emergence of [[Yoshida Kanetomo]]'s sect, {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en|Yoshida Shintō|WD=Q1760351|lt=Yoshida Shintō|1=Yoshida Shintō}}. The term Shinto started to be used with today's meaning of ''kami'' worship only later during the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}.<ref name="Grundbegriffe:Shinto">{{cite web|last=Scheid, Bernhard|author-link=Bernhard Scheid|title=Shintō, Versuch einer Begriffsbestimmung|url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Grundbegriffe/Shinto|access-date=2022-04-21}}</ref> During the same era, {{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|WD=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku|1=Kokugaku}} theorists like {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|WD=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga|1=Motoori Norinaga}} tried to separate it intellectually from Buddhism, preparing the ground for the final schism of the [[Meiji Restoration]].
According to the first view, then, the two religions were at the time of their first meeting already formed and independent and thereafter just coexisted with non-essential exchanges. According to the second, Buddhism, meeting local kami beliefs in Japan, actually produced today's Shinto.<ref name="sueki2">Sueki (2007:2)</ref><ref name="rambelli"/><ref name="Kur7">Kuroda (1981:7)</ref><ref name="ANHS">{{cite book|last=John Breen|first=Mark Teeuwen|title=A new History of Shinto|year=2010|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell|isbn=978-1-4051-5516-8|pages=221}}</ref>
===Assimilation process=== [[File:Japan, Kamakura period - Shotoku Taishi and His Sons - 1964.278 - Cleveland Museum of Art.tif|thumb|{{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}}, an early proponent of Buddhism and instrumental in the defeat of the Mononobe Clan.]] The fusion of Buddhism with the local kami worship started as soon as the first arrived in Japan. [[Mononobe clan|Mononobe]] no Okoshi wrote, "The kami of our land will be offended if we worship a foreign kami."<ref name="Tamura">Tamura, pages 26 to 33.</ref> Mononobe saw {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Gautama Buddha|1=The Buddha}} as just another kami.<ref name="Tamura"/> Foreign kami were called {{nihongo|''banshin''|蕃神|"barbarian gods"}} or {{nihongo|''busshin''|仏神|"Buddhist gods"}}, and understood to be more or less like local ones.<ref name="coka"/> Initially, therefore, the conflict between the two religions was political, and not religious, in nature, a struggle between the progressive [[Soga clan]], that wanted a more international outlook for the country, and the conservative Mononobe clan, that wanted the contrary.<ref name="Tamura"/>
Buddhism was not passive in the assimilation process, but was itself ready to assimilate and be assimilated. By the time it entered Japan, it was already syncretic, having adapted to and amalgamated with other religions and cultures in India, China, and the {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korean Peninsula|1=Korea}}.<ref name="coka">Encyclopedia of Shinto, [https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9715 Combinatory Kami], accessed on October 13, 2008. Quotation: "Buddhism was already product of a complex process of adaptation and amalgamation with other belief systems in India, China, and the Korean peninsula."</ref> For example, already while in India, it had absorbed Hindu divinities like {{ill|Brahma|en|Brahma|WD=Q11389|lt=Brahma|1=Brahma}} (''Bonten'' in Japanese) and {{ill|Indra|en|Indra|WD=Q128335|lt=Indra|1=Indra}} (''Taishakuten'').<ref name="coka"/> When it arrived in Japan, it already had a disposition towards producing the combinatory gods that the Japanese would call {{nihongo|syncretic deities|習合神|shūgōshin}}.<ref name="coka"/> Searching for the origins of a kami in Buddhist scriptures was felt to be nothing out of the ordinary.<ref name="coka"/>
However, if monks didn't doubt the existence of kami, they certainly saw them as inferior to their buddhas.<ref name="scheid">{{cite web |last1=Scheid |first1=Bernhard |title=Honji suijaku: Die Angleichung von Buddhas und kami |url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Geschichte/Honji_suijaku |access-date=21 April 2022 |language=de}}</ref> Hindu gods had already been treated analogously: they had been thought of as unenlightened and prisoners of ''{{ill|Saṃsāra|en|Saṃsāra|WD=Q173324|lt=Saṃsāra|1=Saṃsāra}}''.<ref name="scheid"/> Buddhist claims of superiority encountered resistance, and monks tried to overcome them by deliberately integrating kami into their belief system.<ref name="scheid"/> Several strategies to do this were developed and deployed.<ref name="scheid"/>
The process of amalgamation is usually divided into three stages.<ref name="BT95">Mark Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:95-96)</ref>
The first articulation of the difference between Japanese religious ideas and Buddhism, and the first effort to reconcile the two is attributed to {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}} (574–622), and the first signs that the differences between the two world views were beginning to become manifest to the Japanese in general appear at the time of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu}} (673–86).<ref name="Tamura"/> Accordingly, one of the first efforts to reconcile Shinto and Buddhism was made in the 8th century during the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}} founding so-called {{nihongo|''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}''|神宮寺}}, that is ''shrine-temples'', complexes comprising both a shrine and a temple.<ref name="BT95"/><ref name="EoS">Satō Makoto</ref>
Behind the inclusion in a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} of Buddhist religious objects was the idea that the kami were {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|en|Deva (Buddhism)|WD=Q4089509|lt=lost beings in need of liberation|1=Deva (Buddhism)}} through Buddhism like any other {{ill|Sentient beings (Buddhism)|en|Sentient beings (Buddhism)|WD=Q15276545|lt=sentient beings|1=Sentient beings (Buddhism)}}.<ref name="EoS"/> Kami were thought to be subject to {{ill|Karma in Buddhism|en|Karma in Buddhism|WD=Q2673416|lt=karma|1=Karma in Buddhism}} and {{ill|Rebirth (Buddhism)|en|Rebirth (Buddhism)|WD=Q1480392|lt=reincarnation|1=Rebirth (Buddhism)}} like human beings, and early Buddhist stories tell how the task of helping suffering kami was assumed by {{ill|Dhutanga|en|Dhutanga|WD=Q667466|lt=wandering monks|1=Dhutanga}}.<ref name="scheid"/> A local kami would appear in a dream to the monk, telling him about his suffering.<ref name="scheid"/> To improve the kami's karma through {{ill|Transfer of merit|en|Transfer of merit|WD=Q7137572|lt=rites|1=Transfer of merit}} and the {{ill|Buddhist chant|en|Buddhist chant|WD=Q28163991|lt=recitation of sutras|1=Buddhist chant}}, {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=Buddhist monks|1=Bhikkhu}} would build Buddhist temples next to kami shrines.<ref name="scheid"/> Such groupings had been created by the 7th century, for example at [[Usa Jingū]] in [[Kyushu|Kyūshū]],<ref name="scheid"/> where [[Hachiman]] was worshiped together with [[Maitreya]]. The building of temples at shrines produced {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=shrine-temple|1=Jingū-ji}} complexes, which in turn accelerated the amalgamation process.<ref name="BT95"/> As a result of the creation of shrine-temple complexes, many shrines that had until then been just an open-air site became Buddhist style groupings of buildings.<ref name="NHoS">{{cite book|last=Breen, Teeuwen|title=A New History of Shinto|url=https://archive.org/details/newhistoryshinto00bree_703|url-access=limited|year=2010|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |isbn=978-1-4051-5516-8|pages=[https://archive.org/details/newhistoryshinto00bree_703/page/n52 39]}}</ref>
At the end of the same century, in what is considered the second stage of the amalgamation, the kami Hachiman was declared a {{ill|Dharmapala|en|Dharmapala|WD=Q1207630|lt=Dharmapala|1=Dharmapala}} and, later, a {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva|1=Bodhisattva}}.<ref name="BT95"/> Shrines for him started to be built at temples (the so-called "{{ill|Chinjusha|en|Chinjusha|WD=Q13479654|lt=temple-shrines|1=Chinjusha}}"), marking an important step ahead in the process of amalgamation of kami and Buddhism.<ref name="BT95"/> When the great buddha at [[Tōdai-ji]] in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara|1=Nara (city)}} was built, there was also erected within the temple grounds a shrine for Hachiman – according to the legend because of a wish expressed by the kami himself.<ref name="scheid"/> Hachiman considered this his reward for having helped the temple find the gold and copper mines from which the metal for the great statue had come.<ref name="scheid"/> After this, temples in the entire country adopted tutelary [[kami]] ({{nihongo|chinju|鎮守/鎮主}}.<ref name="BT95"/>
===''Honji suijaku'' theory=== {{main article|Honji suijaku}} The third and final stage of the fusion took place in the 9th century with the development of the {{nihongo|''[[honji suijaku]]''|本地垂迹}} theory according to which Japanese kami are emanations of {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha|1=Buddhahood}}s, ''bodhisattvas'' or {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|en|Deva (Buddhism)|WD=Q4089509|lt=deva|1=Deva (Buddhism)}}s who mingle with human beings to lead them to the Buddhist Way.<ref name="BT95"/> This theory was the keystone of the whole ''shinbutsu shūgō'' edifice and therefore the foundation of Japanese religion for many centuries. Because of it, most kami changed from potentially dangerous spirits to be improved through contact with the Buddhist law to local emanations of buddhas and bodhisattvas which possess wisdom of their own.<ref name="BT95"/> Buddhas and kami were now indivisible twins.<ref name="EoS"/>
The status of kami however changed dramatically according to the sect. At one extreme one was {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism|1=Shingon Buddhism}}'s [[Muromachi period#Shinto|Ryōbu Shintō]] thinkers, who considered kami and buddhas equivalent in power and dignity.<ref name="scheid2">{{cite web |last1=Scheid |first1=Bernhard |title=Shinto im Mittelalter |url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Geschichte/Shinto_Mittelalter |access-date=21 April 2022 |language=en}}</ref> However, not all kami were emanations of some buddha. Some, often called {{nihongo|''jitsu no kami''|実神|true kami}}, usually dangerous and angry, had no Buddhist counterpart. Among them were the ''{{ill|Tengu|en|Tengu|WD=Q742360|lt=Tengu|1=Tengu}}'', or animals possessing magic, as the {{ill|Fox|en|Fox|WD=Q8331|lt=Fox|1=Fox}} (''{{ill|Kitsune|en|Kitsune|WD=Q692111|lt=Kitsune|1=Kitsune}}'') or {{nihongo|[[Japanese raccoon dog#In folklore and tradition|Japanese raccoon dog]]|狸|tanuki}}. Even these unholy and inferior "true kami" however attracted the attention of Ryōbu Shinto thinkers, which resulted in theories which declared them to be manifestations of {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Vairocana|1=Vairocana}} and [[Amaterasu]].<ref name="scheid2"/>
On the other hand, [[Jōdo Shinshū]], the primary Pure Land sect in Japan, was somewhat different because it at first renounced kami-worship due to the notion that kami were inferior to the buddhas.<ref name="scheid2"/> However, the two other {{ill|Pure Land Buddhism|en|Pure Land Buddhism|WD=Q262244|lt=Pure Land|1=Pure Land Buddhism}} schools of [[Jōdo-shū]] and [[Ippen|Ji-shu]] still encouraged the worship of kami despite the fact that the {{ill|Nianfo|en|Nianfo|WD=Q1315754|lt=nembutsu|1=Nianfo}} and trust in Amida Buddha should be the primary practices. Furthermore, under the influence of Rennyo and other leaders, Jōdo Shinshū would later accept the mainstream honji suijaku beliefs and the spiritual relationship between kami and the buddhas and bodhisattvas.<ref>Kenneth Doo Lee (2007), ''The Prince and the Monk: Shotoku Worship in Shinran's Buddhism''; James C. Dobbins (1989), ''Jodo Shinshu: Shin Buddhism in Medieval Japan'', pp. 142-143.</ref>
===Shinbutsu kakuri=== {{main article|Shinbutsu kakuri}}
The two religions however never fused completely and, while overlapping here and there, kept their particular identity within a difficult, largely un-systematized and tense relationship.<ref name="sueki7">Sueki (2007:7-8)</ref> This relationship existed, rather than between two systems, between particular kami and particular buddhas.<ref name="sueki7"/> The two were always perceived as parallel but separate entities.<ref name="ramte"/> Besides ''shinbutsu shūgō'' there was always the other side of the coin of continued separation.<ref name="sueki7"/>
In fact, the term {{nihongo|''shinbutsu kakuri''|神仏隔離|isolation of "[[kami]]" from {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}}}} in Japanese Buddhist terminology refers to the tendency that existed in Japan to keep some kami separate from Buddhism.<ref name="ramte">Rambelli and Teeuwen (2002:21-22)</ref> While some kami were integrated into Buddhism, others (or at times, even the same kami in a different context) were kept systematically away from Buddhism.<ref name="ramte"/> This phenomenon had significant consequences for Japanese culture as a whole.<ref name="ramte"/> It must not be confused with ''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'' ("separation of kami and buddhas") or with ''[[haibutsu kishaku]]'' ("abolish buddhas and destroy Shākyamuni"), which are phenomena recurrent in Japanese history and usually due to political causes. While the first assumes the acceptance of Buddhism, the second and third actually oppose it.
The practice had in any case important consequences, among them the prevention of the complete assimilation of kami practices into Buddhism.<ref name="ramte"/> Also, the prohibition of Buddhism at the Ise and [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]s allowed them to freely develop their theories about the nature of kami.<ref name="ramte"/>
== Buddhism and Shinto after the Separation Order == {{main article|Shinbutsu bunri}} During the ''Shinbutsu bunri'', the attempt to separate Shinto from Buddhism, temples, and shrines were forcefully separated by law with the {{nihongo|"Kami and Buddhism Separation Order"|神仏判然令|Shinbutsu Hanzenrei}} of 1868.
However, despite more than a century of formal separation of the two religions, temples or shrines that do not separate them are still common, as proven for example by the existence of some important Buddhist {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine|1=Inari shrine}}s.<ref>[http://www.toyokawa-map.net/eng/inari.html Toyokawa Inari] accessed on June 6, 2008</ref> During the Meiji period, in order to help the spread of Shinto, shrines with temples (''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}'') were destroyed while temples with shrines (''{{ill|Chinjusha|en|Chinjusha|WD=Q13479654|lt=Chinjusha|1=Chinjusha}}'') were tolerated. As a result, shrines with temples within them are now rare (an extant example is [[Seiganto-ji]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Jungūji|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1126|publisher=Encyclopedia of Shinto|access-date=29 September 2010}}</ref>), but shrines contained within temples are common, and most temples still have at least a small one.<ref name="BT7">Breen and Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:7)</ref>
Prominent religious institutions in both camps still give evidence of integration of the two religions. The great [[Kenchō-ji]] temple, number one of the {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura}}'s great {{ill|Zen|en|Zen|WD=Q7953|lt=Zen|1=Zen}} temples (the {{ill|Five Mountain System|en|Five Mountain System|WD=Q44372|lt=Five Mountain System|1=Five Mountain System}}) includes two shrines. One of the islands in the right-side pond of [[Tsurugaoka Hachimangū]] in Kamakura hosts a sub shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a form of [[Saraswati]].<ref name="Kamiya18"/> For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinbutsu Bunri'', but rebuilt in 1956.<ref name="Kamiya18">Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19)</ref>
Shinto and Buddhism still have a symbiotic relationship of interdependence, particularly concerning funeral rites (entrusted to Buddhism) and {{ill|Marriage in Japan|en|Marriage in Japan|WD=Q6772869|lt=weddings|1=Marriage in Japan}} (usually left to Shinto or sometimes Christianity). The separation of the two religions is therefore considered only superficial, and ''shinbutsu shūgō'' is still an accepted practice.
Still, the separation of the two religions is felt to be real by the public. Scholar Karen Smyers comments, "The surprise of many of my informants regarding the existence of Buddhist Inari temples shows the success of the government's attempt to create separate conceptual categories regarding sites and certain identities, although practice remains multiple and nonexclusive".<ref>Smyers, pag. 219</ref>

{{Short description|Japanese syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism}} {{Italic title|reason=}} {{Shinto}}{{Refimprove|date=October 2023}}[[File:Inari-Jogyo-ji.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Kitsune|en|Kitsune|WD=Q692111|lt=Foxes|1=Kitsune}} sacred to Shinto kami {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|WD=Q719665|lt=Inari|1=Inari Ōkami}}, a ''[[torii]]'', a Buddhist [[Japanese pagoda|stone pagoda]], and Buddhist figures together at Jōgyō-ji, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura}}.]] '''''Shinbutsu-shūgō''''' ({{lang|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}, "syncretism of [[kami]] and buddhas"), also called '''Shinbutsu shū''' ({{lang|ja|神仏宗}}, "kami and {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=The Buddha|1=The Buddha}} school") '''Shinbutsu-konkō''' ({{lang|ja|神仏混淆}}, "jumbling up" or "contamination of kami and buddhas"), is the {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=Syncretism|1=Syncretism}} of [[Shinto]] and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}} that was Japan's main organized religion up until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period|1=Meiji era}}. Beginning in 1868, the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government|1=Government of Meiji Japan}} approved a series of laws that separated Japanese native [[kami]] worship, on one side, from Buddhism which had assimilated it, on the other.
When Buddhism was introduced from {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China|1=China}} in the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|WD=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}} (6th century), the Japanese tried to reconcile the new beliefs with the older [[Shinto]] beliefs, assuming both were true. As a consequence, {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples|1=Buddhist temples in Japan}} ({{lang|ja|寺}}, ''tera'') were {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=attached|1=Jingū-ji}} to local {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}}s ({{lang|ja|神社}}, ''jinja'') and vice versa and devoted to both [[kami]] and {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=Buddhist figures|1=Buddhahood}}. The local religion and foreign Buddhism never fused into a single, unified religion, but remained inextricably linked to the present day through interaction. The depth of the influence from Buddhism on local religious beliefs can be seen in much of Shinto's conceptual vocabulary and even the types of Shinto shrines seen today. The large worship halls and religious images are themselves of Buddhist origin.<ref name="Tamura21">Tamura, page 21</ref> The formal [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Buddhism from Shinto]] took place only as recently as the end of the 19th century; however, in many ways, the blending of the two still continues.<ref name="sueki2"/>
The term ''shinbutsu shūgō'' itself was coined during the early modern era (17th century) to refer to the amalgamation of kami and buddhas in general, as opposed to specific currents within Buddhism which did the same, e.g. Ryōbu Shintō and Sannō Shintō.<ref name=inoue>Inoue (2004:67-68)</ref> The term may have a negative connotation of bastardization and randomness.<ref>Teeuwen & Rambelli (2002:49)</ref> It is a {{ill|Yojijukugo|en|Yojijukugo|WD=Q7010524|lt=Yojijukugo|1=Yojijukugo}} phrase.
==Assimilation of Buddhism==
===Debate over the nature of Shinto=== There is no agreement among specialists as to the exact extent of fusion between the two religions.<ref name="BT4"/>
According to some scholars (such as Hirai Naofusa in Japan and {{ill|Joseph Kitagawa|en|Joseph Kitagawa|WD=Q3185165|lt=Joseph Kitagawa|1=Joseph Kitagawa}} in the US), Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, has existed as such continuously since its prehistory, and consists of all the uniquely Japanese rituals and beliefs shaped by Japanese history from prehistory to the present.<ref name="BT4"/> The term "Shinto" itself was coined in the 6th century to differentiate the previously disparate local religious practices from imported Buddhism.<ref name="KG139">Kitagawa (1987:139)</ref>
The opposing view of Japanese historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en|Toshio Kuroda|WD=Q130309955|lt=Toshio Kuroda|1=Toshio Kuroda}}<ref>{{citation |last=Kuroda |first=Toshio |contribution=Shinto in the History of Japanese Religion |date=1981 |contribution-url=http://www.univie.ac.at/rel_jap/k/images/0/03/Kuroda_1981.pdf |translator-last=Dobbins |translator-first=James C. |translator2-last=Gay |translator2-first=Suzanne |display-translators=1 |title=Journal of Japanese Studies |volume=7 |issue=1 }}.</ref> and his supporters is that Shinto as an independent religion was born only in the modern period after emerging in the Middle Ages as an offshoot of Buddhism,<ref name="BT4">Breen and Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:4-5)</ref><ref name="rambelli">Rambelli (2001)</ref> and that Shinto as a distinct religion is a Meiji era invention of Japanese nationalist ideologues.<ref name="BT4"/> Kuroda points out how the state formalization of ''[[kami]]'' rituals and the state Ranking of shrines during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} were not the emergence of Shinto as an independent religion, but an effort to explain local beliefs in Buddhist terms.<ref name="BT4"/> He also says that, while it is true that the two characters for "Shinto" appear very early in the historical record (for example in the [[Nihon Shoki]]), this does not mean today's Shinto already existed as a religion because the same word was originally used for [[Taoism]] or even for religion in general.<ref name="BT4"/> Indeed, according to Kuroda, many features of Shinto (for example the worshiping of mirrors and swords or the very structure of the [[Ise Grand Shrine]], Shinto's holiest and most important site) are typical of Taoism.<ref name="BT4"/> The term "Shinto" in old texts, therefore, does not necessarily indicate something uniquely Japanese.
Still, according to this view, Shinto's rise as an autonomous religion was gradual and started to become evident with the emergence of [[Yoshida Kanetomo]]'s sect, {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en|Yoshida Shintō|WD=Q1760351|lt=Yoshida Shintō|1=Yoshida Shintō}}. The term Shinto started to be used with today's meaning of ''kami'' worship only later during the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}.<ref name="Grundbegriffe:Shinto">{{cite web|last=Scheid, Bernhard|author-link=Bernhard Scheid|title=Shintō, Versuch einer Begriffsbestimmung|url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Grundbegriffe/Shinto|access-date=2022-04-21}}</ref> During the same era, {{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|WD=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku|1=Kokugaku}} theorists like {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|WD=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga|1=Motoori Norinaga}} tried to separate it intellectually from Buddhism, preparing the ground for the final schism of the [[Meiji Restoration]].
According to the first view, then, the two religions were at the time of their first meeting already formed and independent and thereafter just coexisted with non-essential exchanges. According to the second, Buddhism, meeting local kami beliefs in Japan, actually produced today's Shinto.<ref name="sueki2">Sueki (2007:2)</ref><ref name="rambelli"/><ref name="Kur7">Kuroda (1981:7)</ref><ref name="ANHS">{{cite book|last=John Breen|first=Mark Teeuwen|title=A new History of Shinto|year=2010|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell|isbn=978-1-4051-5516-8|pages=221}}</ref>
===Assimilation process=== [[File:Japan, Kamakura period - Shotoku Taishi and His Sons - 1964.278 - Cleveland Museum of Art.tif|thumb|{{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}}, an early proponent of Buddhism and instrumental in the defeat of the Mononobe Clan.]] The fusion of Buddhism with the local kami worship started as soon as the first arrived in Japan. [[Mononobe clan|Mononobe]] no Okoshi wrote, "The kami of our land will be offended if we worship a foreign kami."<ref name="Tamura">Tamura, pages 26 to 33.</ref> Mononobe saw {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Gautama Buddha|1=The Buddha}} as just another kami.<ref name="Tamura"/> Foreign kami were called {{nihongo|''banshin''|蕃神|"barbarian gods"}} or {{nihongo|''busshin''|仏神|"Buddhist gods"}}, and understood to be more or less like local ones.<ref name="coka"/> Initially, therefore, the conflict between the two religions was political, and not religious, in nature, a struggle between the progressive [[Soga clan]], that wanted a more international outlook for the country, and the conservative Mononobe clan, that wanted the contrary.<ref name="Tamura"/>
Buddhism was not passive in the assimilation process, but was itself ready to assimilate and be assimilated. By the time it entered Japan, it was already syncretic, having adapted to and amalgamated with other religions and cultures in India, China, and the {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korean Peninsula|1=Korea}}.<ref name="coka">Encyclopedia of Shinto, [https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9715 Combinatory Kami], accessed on October 13, 2008. Quotation: "Buddhism was already product of a complex process of adaptation and amalgamation with other belief systems in India, China, and the Korean peninsula."</ref> For example, already while in India, it had absorbed Hindu divinities like {{ill|Brahma|en|Brahma|WD=Q11389|lt=Brahma|1=Brahma}} (''Bonten'' in Japanese) and {{ill|Indra|en|Indra|WD=Q128335|lt=Indra|1=Indra}} (''Taishakuten'').<ref name="coka"/> When it arrived in Japan, it already had a disposition towards producing the combinatory gods that the Japanese would call {{nihongo|syncretic deities|習合神|shūgōshin}}.<ref name="coka"/> Searching for the origins of a kami in Buddhist scriptures was felt to be nothing out of the ordinary.<ref name="coka"/>
However, if monks didn't doubt the existence of kami, they certainly saw them as inferior to their buddhas.<ref name="scheid">{{cite web |last1=Scheid |first1=Bernhard |title=Honji suijaku: Die Angleichung von Buddhas und kami |url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Geschichte/Honji_suijaku |access-date=21 April 2022 |language=de}}</ref> Hindu gods had already been treated analogously: they had been thought of as unenlightened and prisoners of ''{{ill|Saṃsāra|en|Saṃsāra|WD=Q173324|lt=Saṃsāra|1=Saṃsāra}}''.<ref name="scheid"/> Buddhist claims of superiority encountered resistance, and monks tried to overcome them by deliberately integrating kami into their belief system.<ref name="scheid"/> Several strategies to do this were developed and deployed.<ref name="scheid"/>
The process of amalgamation is usually divided into three stages.<ref name="BT95">Mark Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:95-96)</ref>
The first articulation of the difference between Japanese religious ideas and Buddhism, and the first effort to reconcile the two is attributed to {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}} (574–622), and the first signs that the differences between the two world views were beginning to become manifest to the Japanese in general appear at the time of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu}} (673–86).<ref name="Tamura"/> Accordingly, one of the first efforts to reconcile Shinto and Buddhism was made in the 8th century during the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}} founding so-called {{nihongo|''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}''|神宮寺}}, that is ''shrine-temples'', complexes comprising both a shrine and a temple.<ref name="BT95"/><ref name="EoS">Satō Makoto</ref>
Behind the inclusion in a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} of Buddhist religious objects was the idea that the kami were {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|en|Deva (Buddhism)|WD=Q4089509|lt=lost beings in need of liberation|1=Deva (Buddhism)}} through Buddhism like any other {{ill|Sentient beings (Buddhism)|en|Sentient beings (Buddhism)|WD=Q15276545|lt=sentient beings|1=Sentient beings (Buddhism)}}.<ref name="EoS"/> Kami were thought to be subject to {{ill|Karma in Buddhism|en|Karma in Buddhism|WD=Q2673416|lt=karma|1=Karma in Buddhism}} and {{ill|Rebirth (Buddhism)|en|Rebirth (Buddhism)|WD=Q1480392|lt=reincarnation|1=Rebirth (Buddhism)}} like human beings, and early Buddhist stories tell how the task of helping suffering kami was assumed by {{ill|Dhutanga|en|Dhutanga|WD=Q667466|lt=wandering monks|1=Dhutanga}}.<ref name="scheid"/> A local kami would appear in a dream to the monk, telling him about his suffering.<ref name="scheid"/> To improve the kami's karma through {{ill|Transfer of merit|en|Transfer of merit|WD=Q7137572|lt=rites|1=Transfer of merit}} and the {{ill|Buddhist chant|en|Buddhist chant|WD=Q28163991|lt=recitation of sutras|1=Buddhist chant}}, {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=Buddhist monks|1=Bhikkhu}} would build Buddhist temples next to kami shrines.<ref name="scheid"/> Such groupings had been created by the 7th century, for example at [[Usa Jingū]] in [[Kyushu|Kyūshū]],<ref name="scheid"/> where [[Hachiman]] was worshiped together with [[Maitreya]]. The building of temples at shrines produced {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=shrine-temple|1=Jingū-ji}} complexes, which in turn accelerated the amalgamation process.<ref name="BT95"/> As a result of the creation of shrine-temple complexes, many shrines that had until then been just an open-air site became Buddhist style groupings of buildings.<ref name="NHoS">{{cite book|last=Breen, Teeuwen|title=A New History of Shinto|url=https://archive.org/details/newhistoryshinto00bree_703|url-access=limited|year=2010|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |isbn=978-1-4051-5516-8|pages=[https://archive.org/details/newhistoryshinto00bree_703/page/n52 39]}}</ref>
At the end of the same century, in what is considered the second stage of the amalgamation, the kami Hachiman was declared a {{ill|Dharmapala|en|Dharmapala|WD=Q1207630|lt=Dharmapala|1=Dharmapala}} and, later, a {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva|1=Bodhisattva}}.<ref name="BT95"/> Shrines for him started to be built at temples (the so-called "{{ill|Chinjusha|en|Chinjusha|WD=Q13479654|lt=temple-shrines|1=Chinjusha}}"), marking an important step ahead in the process of amalgamation of kami and Buddhism.<ref name="BT95"/> When the great buddha at [[Tōdai-ji]] in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara|1=Nara (city)}} was built, there was also erected within the temple grounds a shrine for Hachiman – according to the legend because of a wish expressed by the kami himself.<ref name="scheid"/> Hachiman considered this his reward for having helped the temple find the gold and copper mines from which the metal for the great statue had come.<ref name="scheid"/> After this, temples in the entire country adopted tutelary [[kami]] ({{nihongo|chinju|鎮守/鎮主}}.<ref name="BT95"/>
===''Honji suijaku'' theory=== {{main article|Honji suijaku}} The third and final stage of the fusion took place in the 9th century with the development of the {{nihongo|''[[honji suijaku]]''|本地垂迹}} theory according to which Japanese kami are emanations of {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha|1=Buddhahood}}s, ''bodhisattvas'' or {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|en|Deva (Buddhism)|WD=Q4089509|lt=deva|1=Deva (Buddhism)}}s who mingle with human beings to lead them to the Buddhist Way.<ref name="BT95"/> This theory was the keystone of the whole ''shinbutsu shūgō'' edifice and therefore the foundation of Japanese religion for many centuries. Because of it, most kami changed from potentially dangerous spirits to be improved through contact with the Buddhist law to local emanations of buddhas and bodhisattvas which possess wisdom of their own.<ref name="BT95"/> Buddhas and kami were now indivisible twins.<ref name="EoS"/>
The status of kami however changed dramatically according to the sect. At one extreme one was {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism|1=Shingon Buddhism}}'s [[Muromachi period#Shinto|Ryōbu Shintō]] thinkers, who considered kami and buddhas equivalent in power and dignity.<ref name="scheid2">{{cite web |last1=Scheid |first1=Bernhard |title=Shinto im Mittelalter |url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Geschichte/Shinto_Mittelalter |access-date=21 April 2022 |language=en}}</ref> However, not all kami were emanations of some buddha. Some, often called {{nihongo|''jitsu no kami''|実神|true kami}}, usually dangerous and angry, had no Buddhist counterpart. Among them were the ''{{ill|Tengu|en|Tengu|WD=Q742360|lt=Tengu|1=Tengu}}'', or animals possessing magic, as the {{ill|Fox|en|Fox|WD=Q8331|lt=Fox|1=Fox}} (''{{ill|Kitsune|en|Kitsune|WD=Q692111|lt=Kitsune|1=Kitsune}}'') or {{nihongo|[[Japanese raccoon dog#In folklore and tradition|Japanese raccoon dog]]|狸|tanuki}}. Even these unholy and inferior "true kami" however attracted the attention of Ryōbu Shinto thinkers, which resulted in theories which declared them to be manifestations of {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Vairocana|1=Vairocana}} and [[Amaterasu]].<ref name="scheid2"/>
On the other hand, [[Jōdo Shinshū]], the primary Pure Land sect in Japan, was somewhat different because it at first renounced kami-worship due to the notion that kami were inferior to the buddhas.<ref name="scheid2"/> However, the two other {{ill|Pure Land Buddhism|en|Pure Land Buddhism|WD=Q262244|lt=Pure Land|1=Pure Land Buddhism}} schools of [[Jōdo-shū]] and [[Ippen|Ji-shu]] still encouraged the worship of kami despite the fact that the {{ill|Nianfo|en|Nianfo|WD=Q1315754|lt=nembutsu|1=Nianfo}} and trust in Amida Buddha should be the primary practices. Furthermore, under the influence of Rennyo and other leaders, Jōdo Shinshū would later accept the mainstream honji suijaku beliefs and the spiritual relationship between kami and the buddhas and bodhisattvas.<ref>Kenneth Doo Lee (2007), ''The Prince and the Monk: Shotoku Worship in Shinran's Buddhism''; James C. Dobbins (1989), ''Jodo Shinshu: Shin Buddhism in Medieval Japan'', pp. 142-143.</ref>
===Shinbutsu kakuri=== {{main article|Shinbutsu kakuri}}
The two religions however never fused completely and, while overlapping here and there, kept their particular identity within a difficult, largely un-systematized and tense relationship.<ref name="sueki7">Sueki (2007:7-8)</ref> This relationship existed, rather than between two systems, between particular kami and particular buddhas.<ref name="sueki7"/> The two were always perceived as parallel but separate entities.<ref name="ramte"/> Besides ''shinbutsu shūgō'' there was always the other side of the coin of continued separation.<ref name="sueki7"/>
In fact, the term {{nihongo|''shinbutsu kakuri''|神仏隔離|isolation of "[[kami]]" from {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}}}} in Japanese Buddhist terminology refers to the tendency that existed in Japan to keep some kami separate from Buddhism.<ref name="ramte">Rambelli and Teeuwen (2002:21-22)</ref> While some kami were integrated into Buddhism, others (or at times, even the same kami in a different context) were kept systematically away from Buddhism.<ref name="ramte"/> This phenomenon had significant consequences for Japanese culture as a whole.<ref name="ramte"/> It must not be confused with ''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'' ("separation of kami and buddhas") or with ''[[haibutsu kishaku]]'' ("abolish buddhas and destroy Shākyamuni"), which are phenomena recurrent in Japanese history and usually due to political causes. While the first assumes the acceptance of Buddhism, the second and third actually oppose it.
The practice had in any case important consequences, among them the prevention of the complete assimilation of kami practices into Buddhism.<ref name="ramte"/> Also, the prohibition of Buddhism at the Ise and [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]s allowed them to freely develop their theories about the nature of kami.<ref name="ramte"/>
== Buddhism and Shinto after the Separation Order == {{main article|Shinbutsu bunri}} During the ''Shinbutsu bunri'', the attempt to separate Shinto from Buddhism, temples, and shrines were forcefully separated by law with the {{nihongo|"Kami and Buddhism Separation Order"|神仏判然令|Shinbutsu Hanzenrei}} of 1868.
However, despite more than a century of formal separation of the two religions, temples or shrines that do not separate them are still common, as proven for example by the existence of some important Buddhist {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine|1=Inari shrine}}s.<ref>[http://www.toyokawa-map.net/eng/inari.html Toyokawa Inari] accessed on June 6, 2008</ref> During the Meiji period, in order to help the spread of Shinto, shrines with temples (''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}'') were destroyed while temples with shrines (''{{ill|Chinjusha|en|Chinjusha|WD=Q13479654|lt=Chinjusha|1=Chinjusha}}'') were tolerated. As a result, shrines with temples within them are now rare (an extant example is [[Seiganto-ji]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Jungūji|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1126|publisher=Encyclopedia of Shinto|access-date=29 September 2010}}</ref>), but shrines contained within temples are common, and most temples still have at least a small one.<ref name="BT7">Breen and Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:7)</ref>
Prominent religious institutions in both camps still give evidence of integration of the two religions. The great [[Kenchō-ji]] temple, number one of the {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura}}'s great {{ill|Zen|en|Zen|WD=Q7953|lt=Zen|1=Zen}} temples (the {{ill|Five Mountain System|en|Five Mountain System|WD=Q44372|lt=Five Mountain System|1=Five Mountain System}}) includes two shrines. One of the islands in the right-side pond of [[Tsurugaoka Hachimangū]] in Kamakura hosts a sub shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a form of [[Saraswati]].<ref name="Kamiya18"/> For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinbutsu Bunri'', but rebuilt in 1956.<ref name="Kamiya18">Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19)</ref>
Shinto and Buddhism still have a symbiotic relationship of interdependence, particularly concerning funeral rites (entrusted to Buddhism) and {{ill|Marriage in Japan|en|Marriage in Japan|WD=Q6772869|lt=weddings|1=Marriage in Japan}} (usually left to Shinto or sometimes Christianity). The separation of the two religions is therefore considered only superficial, and ''shinbutsu shūgō'' is still an accepted practice.
Still, the separation of the two religions is felt to be real by the public. Scholar Karen Smyers comments, "The surprise of many of my informants regarding the existence of Buddhist Inari temples shows the success of the government's attempt to create separate conceptual categories regarding sites and certain identities, although practice remains multiple and nonexclusive".<ref>Smyers, pag. 219</ref>

History (Middle Ages) Research|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1260|encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=10 December 2010}} * {{cite web |url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=826 |title=Shinto and Buddhism — Development of Shinbutsu Shūgō (Combinatory Religion of Kami and buddhas)— |last=Satō |first=Makoto |date=2006-12-09 |access-date=2008-05-12}} * {{cite web |last1=Scheid |first1=Bernhard |author-link=Bernhard Scheid |title=Religion-in-Japan |url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch |website=Religion-in-Japan, ein digitales Handbuch |publisher=Austrian Academy od Sciences, since 2001 |access-date=21 April 2022 |language= de }} *{{cite book |last=Sueki, Fumihiko |author-link=Fumihiko Sueki |title=Chūsei no kami to hotoke |publisher=Yamakawa Shuppansha |location=Tokyo |year=2007 |isbn=978-4-634-54320-1 |language=ja }} *{{cite book |last=Tamura |first=Yoshiro |title=Japanese Buddhism - A Cultural History |publisher=Kosei Publishing Company |location=Tokyo|year=2000 |edition=First |chapter=The Birth of the Japanese nation |isbn=4-333-01684-3|page=232 pages}} * {{cite book | last = Smyers, Karen Ann | author-link = Karen Ann Smyers | title = The Fox and the Jewel: Shared and Private Meanings in Contemporary Japanese Inari Worship | publisher = University of Hawaii Press | year = 1999 | location = Honolulu | isbn = 0-8248-2102-5 | oclc = 231775156 }} * [http://search.japantimes.co.jp/cgi-bin/fb20010715a2.html Dismantling stereotypes surrounding Japan's sacred entities] by Fabio Rambelli, Japan Times, July 15, 2001, excerpted from Monumenta Nipponica, 56:2 * {{cite book |isbn=978-0-415-29747-9 |author=Mark Teeuwen and [[Fabio Rambelli]] (Editors) |date=Dec 27, 2002 |publisher=RoutledgeCurzon |location=London |title=Buddhas and Kami in Japan: Honji Suijaku as a Combinatory Paradigm }}

{{Short description|Japanese syncretism of Shinto and Buddhism}} {{Italic title|reason=}} {{Shinto}}{{Refimprove|date=October 2023}}[[File:Inari-Jogyo-ji.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Kitsune|en|Kitsune|WD=Q692111|lt=Foxes|1=Kitsune}} sacred to Shinto kami {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|WD=Q719665|lt=Inari|1=Inari Ōkami}}, a ''[[torii]]'', a Buddhist [[Japanese pagoda|stone pagoda]], and Buddhist figures together at Jōgyō-ji, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura}}.]] '''''Shinbutsu-shūgō''''' ({{lang|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}, "syncretism of [[kami]] and buddhas"), also called '''Shinbutsu shū''' ({{lang|ja|神仏宗}}, "kami and {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=The Buddha|1=The Buddha}} school") '''Shinbutsu-konkō''' ({{lang|ja|神仏混淆}}, "jumbling up" or "contamination of kami and buddhas"), is the {{ill|Syncretism|en|Syncretism|WD=Q172904|lt=Syncretism|1=Syncretism}} of [[Shinto]] and {{ill|Buddhism in Japan|en|Buddhism in Japan|WD=Q736311|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism in Japan}} that was Japan's main organized religion up until the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji period|1=Meiji era}}. Beginning in 1868, the new {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|WD=Q1322181|lt=Meiji government|1=Government of Meiji Japan}} approved a series of laws that separated Japanese native [[kami]] worship, on one side, from Buddhism which had assimilated it, on the other.
When Buddhism was introduced from {{ill|China|en|China|WD=Q148|lt=China|1=China}} in the {{ill|Asuka period|en|Asuka period|WD=Q210688|lt=Asuka period|1=Asuka period}} (6th century), the Japanese tried to reconcile the new beliefs with the older [[Shinto]] beliefs, assuming both were true. As a consequence, {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temples|1=Buddhist temples in Japan}} ({{lang|ja|寺}}, ''tera'') were {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=attached|1=Jingū-ji}} to local {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}}s ({{lang|ja|神社}}, ''jinja'') and vice versa and devoted to both [[kami]] and {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=Buddhist figures|1=Buddhahood}}. The local religion and foreign Buddhism never fused into a single, unified religion, but remained inextricably linked to the present day through interaction. The depth of the influence from Buddhism on local religious beliefs can be seen in much of Shinto's conceptual vocabulary and even the types of Shinto shrines seen today. The large worship halls and religious images are themselves of Buddhist origin.<ref name="Tamura21">Tamura, page 21</ref> The formal [[Shinbutsu bunri|separation of Buddhism from Shinto]] took place only as recently as the end of the 19th century; however, in many ways, the blending of the two still continues.<ref name="sueki2"/>
The term ''shinbutsu shūgō'' itself was coined during the early modern era (17th century) to refer to the amalgamation of kami and buddhas in general, as opposed to specific currents within Buddhism which did the same, e.g. Ryōbu Shintō and Sannō Shintō.<ref name=inoue>Inoue (2004:67-68)</ref> The term may have a negative connotation of bastardization and randomness.<ref>Teeuwen & Rambelli (2002:49)</ref> It is a {{ill|Yojijukugo|en|Yojijukugo|WD=Q7010524|lt=Yojijukugo|1=Yojijukugo}} phrase.
==Assimilation of Buddhism==
===Debate over the nature of Shinto=== There is no agreement among specialists as to the exact extent of fusion between the two religions.<ref name="BT4"/>
According to some scholars (such as Hirai Naofusa in Japan and {{ill|Joseph Kitagawa|en|Joseph Kitagawa|WD=Q3185165|lt=Joseph Kitagawa|1=Joseph Kitagawa}} in the US), Shinto is the indigenous religion of Japan, has existed as such continuously since its prehistory, and consists of all the uniquely Japanese rituals and beliefs shaped by Japanese history from prehistory to the present.<ref name="BT4"/> The term "Shinto" itself was coined in the 6th century to differentiate the previously disparate local religious practices from imported Buddhism.<ref name="KG139">Kitagawa (1987:139)</ref>
The opposing view of Japanese historian {{ill|Toshio Kuroda|en|Toshio Kuroda|WD=Q130309955|lt=Toshio Kuroda|1=Toshio Kuroda}}<ref>{{citation |last=Kuroda |first=Toshio |contribution=Shinto in the History of Japanese Religion |date=1981 |contribution-url=http://www.univie.ac.at/rel_jap/k/images/0/03/Kuroda_1981.pdf |translator-last=Dobbins |translator-first=James C. |translator2-last=Gay |translator2-first=Suzanne |display-translators=1 |title=Journal of Japanese Studies |volume=7 |issue=1 }}.</ref> and his supporters is that Shinto as an independent religion was born only in the modern period after emerging in the Middle Ages as an offshoot of Buddhism,<ref name="BT4">Breen and Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:4-5)</ref><ref name="rambelli">Rambelli (2001)</ref> and that Shinto as a distinct religion is a Meiji era invention of Japanese nationalist ideologues.<ref name="BT4"/> Kuroda points out how the state formalization of ''[[kami]]'' rituals and the state Ranking of shrines during the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} were not the emergence of Shinto as an independent religion, but an effort to explain local beliefs in Buddhist terms.<ref name="BT4"/> He also says that, while it is true that the two characters for "Shinto" appear very early in the historical record (for example in the [[Nihon Shoki]]), this does not mean today's Shinto already existed as a religion because the same word was originally used for [[Taoism]] or even for religion in general.<ref name="BT4"/> Indeed, according to Kuroda, many features of Shinto (for example the worshiping of mirrors and swords or the very structure of the [[Ise Grand Shrine]], Shinto's holiest and most important site) are typical of Taoism.<ref name="BT4"/> The term "Shinto" in old texts, therefore, does not necessarily indicate something uniquely Japanese.
Still, according to this view, Shinto's rise as an autonomous religion was gradual and started to become evident with the emergence of [[Yoshida Kanetomo]]'s sect, {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en|Yoshida Shintō|WD=Q1760351|lt=Yoshida Shintō|1=Yoshida Shintō}}. The term Shinto started to be used with today's meaning of ''kami'' worship only later during the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}.<ref name="Grundbegriffe:Shinto">{{cite web|last=Scheid, Bernhard|author-link=Bernhard Scheid|title=Shintō, Versuch einer Begriffsbestimmung|url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Grundbegriffe/Shinto|access-date=2022-04-21}}</ref> During the same era, {{ill|Kokugaku|en|Kokugaku|WD=Q855159|lt=Kokugaku|1=Kokugaku}} theorists like {{ill|Motoori Norinaga|en|Motoori Norinaga|WD=Q384647|lt=Motoori Norinaga|1=Motoori Norinaga}} tried to separate it intellectually from Buddhism, preparing the ground for the final schism of the [[Meiji Restoration]].
According to the first view, then, the two religions were at the time of their first meeting already formed and independent and thereafter just coexisted with non-essential exchanges. According to the second, Buddhism, meeting local kami beliefs in Japan, actually produced today's Shinto.<ref name="sueki2">Sueki (2007:2)</ref><ref name="rambelli"/><ref name="Kur7">Kuroda (1981:7)</ref><ref name="ANHS">{{cite book|last=John Breen|first=Mark Teeuwen|title=A new History of Shinto|year=2010|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell|isbn=978-1-4051-5516-8|pages=221}}</ref>
===Assimilation process=== [[File:Japan, Kamakura period - Shotoku Taishi and His Sons - 1964.278 - Cleveland Museum of Art.tif|thumb|{{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}}, an early proponent of Buddhism and instrumental in the defeat of the Mononobe Clan.]] The fusion of Buddhism with the local kami worship started as soon as the first arrived in Japan. [[Mononobe clan|Mononobe]] no Okoshi wrote, "The kami of our land will be offended if we worship a foreign kami."<ref name="Tamura">Tamura, pages 26 to 33.</ref> Mononobe saw {{ill|The Buddha|en|The Buddha|WD=Q9441|lt=Gautama Buddha|1=The Buddha}} as just another kami.<ref name="Tamura"/> Foreign kami were called {{nihongo|''banshin''|蕃神|"barbarian gods"}} or {{nihongo|''busshin''|仏神|"Buddhist gods"}}, and understood to be more or less like local ones.<ref name="coka"/> Initially, therefore, the conflict between the two religions was political, and not religious, in nature, a struggle between the progressive [[Soga clan]], that wanted a more international outlook for the country, and the conservative Mononobe clan, that wanted the contrary.<ref name="Tamura"/>
Buddhism was not passive in the assimilation process, but was itself ready to assimilate and be assimilated. By the time it entered Japan, it was already syncretic, having adapted to and amalgamated with other religions and cultures in India, China, and the {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korean Peninsula|1=Korea}}.<ref name="coka">Encyclopedia of Shinto, [https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9715 Combinatory Kami], accessed on October 13, 2008. Quotation: "Buddhism was already product of a complex process of adaptation and amalgamation with other belief systems in India, China, and the Korean peninsula."</ref> For example, already while in India, it had absorbed Hindu divinities like {{ill|Brahma|en|Brahma|WD=Q11389|lt=Brahma|1=Brahma}} (''Bonten'' in Japanese) and {{ill|Indra|en|Indra|WD=Q128335|lt=Indra|1=Indra}} (''Taishakuten'').<ref name="coka"/> When it arrived in Japan, it already had a disposition towards producing the combinatory gods that the Japanese would call {{nihongo|syncretic deities|習合神|shūgōshin}}.<ref name="coka"/> Searching for the origins of a kami in Buddhist scriptures was felt to be nothing out of the ordinary.<ref name="coka"/>
However, if monks didn't doubt the existence of kami, they certainly saw them as inferior to their buddhas.<ref name="scheid">{{cite web |last1=Scheid |first1=Bernhard |title=Honji suijaku: Die Angleichung von Buddhas und kami |url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Geschichte/Honji_suijaku |access-date=21 April 2022 |language=de}}</ref> Hindu gods had already been treated analogously: they had been thought of as unenlightened and prisoners of ''{{ill|Saṃsāra|en|Saṃsāra|WD=Q173324|lt=Saṃsāra|1=Saṃsāra}}''.<ref name="scheid"/> Buddhist claims of superiority encountered resistance, and monks tried to overcome them by deliberately integrating kami into their belief system.<ref name="scheid"/> Several strategies to do this were developed and deployed.<ref name="scheid"/>
The process of amalgamation is usually divided into three stages.<ref name="BT95">Mark Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:95-96)</ref>
The first articulation of the difference between Japanese religious ideas and Buddhism, and the first effort to reconcile the two is attributed to {{ill|Prince Shōtoku|en|Prince Shōtoku|WD=Q263972|lt=Prince Shōtoku|1=Prince Shōtoku}} (574–622), and the first signs that the differences between the two world views were beginning to become manifest to the Japanese in general appear at the time of {{ill|Emperor Tenmu|en|Emperor Tenmu|WD=Q335181|lt=Emperor Tenmu|1=Emperor Tenmu}} (673–86).<ref name="Tamura"/> Accordingly, one of the first efforts to reconcile Shinto and Buddhism was made in the 8th century during the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|WD=Q189178|lt=Nara period|1=Nara period}} founding so-called {{nihongo|''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}''|神宮寺}}, that is ''shrine-temples'', complexes comprising both a shrine and a temple.<ref name="BT95"/><ref name="EoS">Satō Makoto</ref>
Behind the inclusion in a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine|1=Shinto shrine}} of Buddhist religious objects was the idea that the kami were {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|en|Deva (Buddhism)|WD=Q4089509|lt=lost beings in need of liberation|1=Deva (Buddhism)}} through Buddhism like any other {{ill|Sentient beings (Buddhism)|en|Sentient beings (Buddhism)|WD=Q15276545|lt=sentient beings|1=Sentient beings (Buddhism)}}.<ref name="EoS"/> Kami were thought to be subject to {{ill|Karma in Buddhism|en|Karma in Buddhism|WD=Q2673416|lt=karma|1=Karma in Buddhism}} and {{ill|Rebirth (Buddhism)|en|Rebirth (Buddhism)|WD=Q1480392|lt=reincarnation|1=Rebirth (Buddhism)}} like human beings, and early Buddhist stories tell how the task of helping suffering kami was assumed by {{ill|Dhutanga|en|Dhutanga|WD=Q667466|lt=wandering monks|1=Dhutanga}}.<ref name="scheid"/> A local kami would appear in a dream to the monk, telling him about his suffering.<ref name="scheid"/> To improve the kami's karma through {{ill|Transfer of merit|en|Transfer of merit|WD=Q7137572|lt=rites|1=Transfer of merit}} and the {{ill|Buddhist chant|en|Buddhist chant|WD=Q28163991|lt=recitation of sutras|1=Buddhist chant}}, {{ill|Bhikkhu|en|Bhikkhu|WD=Q854997|lt=Buddhist monks|1=Bhikkhu}} would build Buddhist temples next to kami shrines.<ref name="scheid"/> Such groupings had been created by the 7th century, for example at [[Usa Jingū]] in [[Kyushu|Kyūshū]],<ref name="scheid"/> where [[Hachiman]] was worshiped together with [[Maitreya]]. The building of temples at shrines produced {{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=shrine-temple|1=Jingū-ji}} complexes, which in turn accelerated the amalgamation process.<ref name="BT95"/> As a result of the creation of shrine-temple complexes, many shrines that had until then been just an open-air site became Buddhist style groupings of buildings.<ref name="NHoS">{{cite book|last=Breen, Teeuwen|title=A New History of Shinto|url=https://archive.org/details/newhistoryshinto00bree_703|url-access=limited|year=2010|publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |isbn=978-1-4051-5516-8|pages=[https://archive.org/details/newhistoryshinto00bree_703/page/n52 39]}}</ref>
At the end of the same century, in what is considered the second stage of the amalgamation, the kami Hachiman was declared a {{ill|Dharmapala|en|Dharmapala|WD=Q1207630|lt=Dharmapala|1=Dharmapala}} and, later, a {{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva|1=Bodhisattva}}.<ref name="BT95"/> Shrines for him started to be built at temples (the so-called "{{ill|Chinjusha|en|Chinjusha|WD=Q13479654|lt=temple-shrines|1=Chinjusha}}"), marking an important step ahead in the process of amalgamation of kami and Buddhism.<ref name="BT95"/> When the great buddha at [[Tōdai-ji]] in {{ill|Nara (city)|en|Nara (city)|WD=Q169134|lt=Nara|1=Nara (city)}} was built, there was also erected within the temple grounds a shrine for Hachiman – according to the legend because of a wish expressed by the kami himself.<ref name="scheid"/> Hachiman considered this his reward for having helped the temple find the gold and copper mines from which the metal for the great statue had come.<ref name="scheid"/> After this, temples in the entire country adopted tutelary [[kami]] ({{nihongo|chinju|鎮守/鎮主}}.<ref name="BT95"/>
===''Honji suijaku'' theory=== {{main article|Honji suijaku}} The third and final stage of the fusion took place in the 9th century with the development of the {{nihongo|''[[honji suijaku]]''|本地垂迹}} theory according to which Japanese kami are emanations of {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha|1=Buddhahood}}s, ''bodhisattvas'' or {{ill|Deva (Buddhism)|en|Deva (Buddhism)|WD=Q4089509|lt=deva|1=Deva (Buddhism)}}s who mingle with human beings to lead them to the Buddhist Way.<ref name="BT95"/> This theory was the keystone of the whole ''shinbutsu shūgō'' edifice and therefore the foundation of Japanese religion for many centuries. Because of it, most kami changed from potentially dangerous spirits to be improved through contact with the Buddhist law to local emanations of buddhas and bodhisattvas which possess wisdom of their own.<ref name="BT95"/> Buddhas and kami were now indivisible twins.<ref name="EoS"/>
The status of kami however changed dramatically according to the sect. At one extreme one was {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism|1=Shingon Buddhism}}'s [[Muromachi period#Shinto|Ryōbu Shintō]] thinkers, who considered kami and buddhas equivalent in power and dignity.<ref name="scheid2">{{cite web |last1=Scheid |first1=Bernhard |title=Shinto im Mittelalter |url=https://religion-in-japan.univie.ac.at/Handbuch/Geschichte/Shinto_Mittelalter |access-date=21 April 2022 |language=en}}</ref> However, not all kami were emanations of some buddha. Some, often called {{nihongo|''jitsu no kami''|実神|true kami}}, usually dangerous and angry, had no Buddhist counterpart. Among them were the ''{{ill|Tengu|en|Tengu|WD=Q742360|lt=Tengu|1=Tengu}}'', or animals possessing magic, as the {{ill|Fox|en|Fox|WD=Q8331|lt=Fox|1=Fox}} (''{{ill|Kitsune|en|Kitsune|WD=Q692111|lt=Kitsune|1=Kitsune}}'') or {{nihongo|[[Japanese raccoon dog#In folklore and tradition|Japanese raccoon dog]]|狸|tanuki}}. Even these unholy and inferior "true kami" however attracted the attention of Ryōbu Shinto thinkers, which resulted in theories which declared them to be manifestations of {{ill|Vairocana|en|Vairocana|WD=Q239847|lt=Vairocana|1=Vairocana}} and [[Amaterasu]].<ref name="scheid2"/>
On the other hand, [[Jōdo Shinshū]], the primary Pure Land sect in Japan, was somewhat different because it at first renounced kami-worship due to the notion that kami were inferior to the buddhas.<ref name="scheid2"/> However, the two other {{ill|Pure Land Buddhism|en|Pure Land Buddhism|WD=Q262244|lt=Pure Land|1=Pure Land Buddhism}} schools of [[Jōdo-shū]] and [[Ippen|Ji-shu]] still encouraged the worship of kami despite the fact that the {{ill|Nianfo|en|Nianfo|WD=Q1315754|lt=nembutsu|1=Nianfo}} and trust in Amida Buddha should be the primary practices. Furthermore, under the influence of Rennyo and other leaders, Jōdo Shinshū would later accept the mainstream honji suijaku beliefs and the spiritual relationship between kami and the buddhas and bodhisattvas.<ref>Kenneth Doo Lee (2007), ''The Prince and the Monk: Shotoku Worship in Shinran's Buddhism''; James C. Dobbins (1989), ''Jodo Shinshu: Shin Buddhism in Medieval Japan'', pp. 142-143.</ref>
===Shinbutsu kakuri=== {{main article|Shinbutsu kakuri}}
The two religions however never fused completely and, while overlapping here and there, kept their particular identity within a difficult, largely un-systematized and tense relationship.<ref name="sueki7">Sueki (2007:7-8)</ref> This relationship existed, rather than between two systems, between particular kami and particular buddhas.<ref name="sueki7"/> The two were always perceived as parallel but separate entities.<ref name="ramte"/> Besides ''shinbutsu shūgō'' there was always the other side of the coin of continued separation.<ref name="sueki7"/>
In fact, the term {{nihongo|''shinbutsu kakuri''|神仏隔離|isolation of "[[kami]]" from {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}}}} in Japanese Buddhist terminology refers to the tendency that existed in Japan to keep some kami separate from Buddhism.<ref name="ramte">Rambelli and Teeuwen (2002:21-22)</ref> While some kami were integrated into Buddhism, others (or at times, even the same kami in a different context) were kept systematically away from Buddhism.<ref name="ramte"/> This phenomenon had significant consequences for Japanese culture as a whole.<ref name="ramte"/> It must not be confused with ''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'' ("separation of kami and buddhas") or with ''[[haibutsu kishaku]]'' ("abolish buddhas and destroy Shākyamuni"), which are phenomena recurrent in Japanese history and usually due to political causes. While the first assumes the acceptance of Buddhism, the second and third actually oppose it.
The practice had in any case important consequences, among them the prevention of the complete assimilation of kami practices into Buddhism.<ref name="ramte"/> Also, the prohibition of Buddhism at the Ise and [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrine]]s allowed them to freely develop their theories about the nature of kami.<ref name="ramte"/>
== Buddhism and Shinto after the Separation Order == {{main article|Shinbutsu bunri}} During the ''Shinbutsu bunri'', the attempt to separate Shinto from Buddhism, temples, and shrines were forcefully separated by law with the {{nihongo|"Kami and Buddhism Separation Order"|神仏判然令|Shinbutsu Hanzenrei}} of 1868.
However, despite more than a century of formal separation of the two religions, temples or shrines that do not separate them are still common, as proven for example by the existence of some important Buddhist {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine|1=Inari shrine}}s.<ref>[http://www.toyokawa-map.net/eng/inari.html Toyokawa Inari] accessed on June 6, 2008</ref> During the Meiji period, in order to help the spread of Shinto, shrines with temples (''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji|1=Jingū-ji}}'') were destroyed while temples with shrines (''{{ill|Chinjusha|en|Chinjusha|WD=Q13479654|lt=Chinjusha|1=Chinjusha}}'') were tolerated. As a result, shrines with temples within them are now rare (an extant example is [[Seiganto-ji]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Jungūji|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1126|publisher=Encyclopedia of Shinto|access-date=29 September 2010}}</ref>), but shrines contained within temples are common, and most temples still have at least a small one.<ref name="BT7">Breen and Teeuwen in ''Breen and Teeuwen'' (2000:7)</ref>
Prominent religious institutions in both camps still give evidence of integration of the two religions. The great [[Kenchō-ji]] temple, number one of the {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura|1=Kamakura}}'s great {{ill|Zen|en|Zen|WD=Q7953|lt=Zen|1=Zen}} temples (the {{ill|Five Mountain System|en|Five Mountain System|WD=Q44372|lt=Five Mountain System|1=Five Mountain System}}) includes two shrines. One of the islands in the right-side pond of [[Tsurugaoka Hachimangū]] in Kamakura hosts a sub shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a form of [[Saraswati]].<ref name="Kamiya18"/> For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinbutsu Bunri'', but rebuilt in 1956.<ref name="Kamiya18">Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19)</ref>
Shinto and Buddhism still have a symbiotic relationship of interdependence, particularly concerning funeral rites (entrusted to Buddhism) and {{ill|Marriage in Japan|en|Marriage in Japan|WD=Q6772869|lt=weddings|1=Marriage in Japan}} (usually left to Shinto or sometimes Christianity). The separation of the two religions is therefore considered only superficial, and ''shinbutsu shūgō'' is still an accepted practice.
Still, the separation of the two religions is felt to be real by the public. Scholar Karen Smyers comments, "The surprise of many of my informants regarding the existence of Buddhist Inari temples shows the success of the government's attempt to create separate conceptual categories regarding sites and certain identities, although practice remains multiple and nonexclusive".<ref>Smyers, pag. 219</ref>
